title: Prompts Don't Govern Agents. Reputation Does.
abstract: AI agents now generate their own decision logic while they work. Zhenfeng Cao argues that this turns the human into an "intent architect" who states goals, lets agents execute, and audits the results. At the scale agents are heading, no human can audit every result. This response proposes a different division of labor. The system judges agent performance around the clock. Assuming reputation for agents is properly calibrated, every agent run leaves a tamper-evident record of what the agent actually did, and agents are graded on held-out work against a standard fixed in advance. An agent turns red only when the evidence shows real underperformance. Red cases go to review, mostly by other agents with their own reputation at stake. Verdicts move standing, standing steers where work goes, and authority tied to tasks expires when the work stops, so the system cleans itself. Reputation never grants permission. The human holds authority, reviews the rare escalated red case, and answers for the outcome.

responds_to.name: Zhenfeng Cao, Agentic Software: How AI Agents Are Restructuring the Software Paradigm (arXiv:2606.05608v2, 2026)

title: After RLHF Comes a Stack, Not a Model
abstract: Calibration is not accountability. A promotional post presents TypeSafe's Jev, a calibrated decision engine trained with Reinforcement Learning for Calibrated Decisions, as what comes after RLHF. The diagnosis is half right: RLHF has a structural flaw, but the flaw is institutional, because whoever supplies the reward signal bears no consequence for being wrong. Calibration cannot by itself replace RLHF: it needs a reference, which is a costless label where no answer key exists; closed-choice outputs redefine hallucination rather than eliminate it; and calibration is a property of populations that someone must keep checking. What comes after RLHF is a stack: verifiable rewards where an answer key exists, calibrated decisions for typed choices, and accountable validation by staked reputation where no key exists. That third layer is proposed, not tested; no policy has yet been trained under it.

responds_to.name: TypeSafe, Introducing System One models and Jev (TypeSafe blog, 2026)

title: Who Vouches for a Dish of Neurons?
abstract: Living neurons can now be rented through the cloud. Their operators monitor them, but nobody publishes a record of which units to trust. A culture can give poor answers, drift or die, and it cannot answer for its mistakes, so the lab that operates it is the natural party to answer. Reputation adds what monitoring lacks: a judge other than the seller, a cost for being wrong, and a reason to perform tomorrow. Standing must not be sold, and a failing unit must not restart under a new name. A basic record can be built now; a fully trustworthy one still needs proof that the readings are real, ground truth where agreement is not enough, a deeper validator pool, and privacy protection for donor cells. Feeding reputation back into the neurons is a research question, not a claim.

responds_to.name: Simon Sharwood, Inside datacenter where day starts with cerebrospinal fluid (The Register, 14 March 2026), reporting the launch of the Cortical Labs biological computing cloud
